source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: a rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: Rational metareasoning picks a strategy by predicting its accuracy and time from problem features. It fits old data as well as SSL, a context-free learning rival, so that data cannot separate them.
numbers: Rieskamp & Otto (2006) Exp 1, 7 blocks of 24 trials: mean squared error 0.0050 (metareasoning) vs 0.0048 (SSL). Fitted: initial bias 0.14, sensitivity 80.
limits: Tie on homogeneous environments. Features were hand-picked by the authors. Fit was to block averages with 2 free parameters.
agent_relevance: A table of expected gain minus cost per problem class is a defensible S0 design. Old data cannot show that features beat plain class averages.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: a rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: Discriminating experiment: a mixed environment where TTB and WADD give opposite answers on every trial. Context-free learners (SSL, RELACS) must score 50%. People scored higher, so selection used problem features.
numbers: N=120 Mechanical Turk, 30 binary loan decisions, 6 criteria. Accuracy 64.6%, 99% credible interval [62.5%, 66.6%]. Context-free prediction 50%. Learning slope CI [-0.1%, 0.2%] per trial (no learning seen). Feedback was 75.96% positive after correct, 25.04% after incorrect.
limits: Only 30 trials and noisy feedback. No learning was detected, so people may have arrived with a skill or used one complex strategy for both kinds of trial. Single online study, no replication found in the sources read. People did worse on non-compensatory trials.
agent_relevance: Evidence that routing should use item features and not only a class-wide average reward. Supports a feature-based S0 over a plain bandit.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: a rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: Simulated Payne et al. (1988) Exp 1: the model predicts more TTB/EBA use under time pressure and high probability dispersion with no feedback. SSL and RELACS predict no difference between conditions.
numbers: Four conditions (15 s limit vs none; low vs high dispersion), 10 problems each, 10 strategies, 1000 simulated learners. Qualitative match only (their Figure 3), no fit statistic.
limits: A simulation against a classic result, not a new human sample. Assumed prior learning history for simulated people.
agent_relevance: A time or token budget should shift the chosen strategy at once, with no new feedback. The router needs the budget as an input feature.

source: Rieskamp (2008) The importance of learning when making inferences (Judgment and Decision Making 3(3))
finding: Reanalysis of Newell, Weston & Shanks (2003): early on people used the costly full-information strategy (WADD) despite high search cost. TTB took over later. This fits learning, and not an up-front cost-benefit choice.
numbers: Stock-inference task, 6 cues, 1 pence per cue search cost vs 7 pence gain; 24 participants; SSL predicted choices with mean probability .71 (SD .05). Newell et al. had classed 11 of 24 as TTB users and 9 as weight-of-evidence users.
limits: Author is the SSL originator and reanalyses with his own theory. Not a pre-registered test. A feature-based cost-benefit account is not ruled out by this.
agent_relevance: People do not start at the cost-optimal strategy. An agent with an expensive prior that learns to cut cost matches humans, so learning is needed and not a fixed rule.

source: Rieskamp (2008) The importance of learning when making inferences (Judgment and Decision Making 3(3))
finding: Reanalysis of Broder & Schiffer (2006) dynamic environments: people adapt slowly and unevenly after the environment changes. SSL predicts slow switching because a strong preference means the rival strategy is rarely tried.
numbers: Phase 1: 79% classed as TTB in the non-compensatory environment, 58% as WADD in the compensatory one. After a switch: only 27% moved to a compensatory strategy, 65% moved to TTB. SSL predicted about 100 extra trials before switching back to WADD; real switching was faster than that.
limits: Strategy classification from choice patterns is noisy. The switch is asymmetric. SSL is also partly refuted since it was too slow.
agent_relevance: Strategy lock-in is real and costly. The router must keep trying the rival strategy, or restart when cost or task type changes.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psychological Review 124)
finding: Main model paper. A search-result summary of its abstract says model comparisons favoured it over SSL, RELACS and SCADS and that four new experiments confirmed distinctive predictions. Full text not opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Primary source for the S0 form (predict strategy performance from features, minus cost). Open it before building.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick & Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control (PLOS Comp Biol 14(4))
finding: The Learned Value of Control model predicts Stroop and Flanker learning and transfer, and beats associative learning and win-stay-lose-shift rivals by BIC.
numbers: On Bugg et al. data: BIC LVOC 1817.8 vs Rescorla-Wagner 9763.2 vs WSLS 3449.9 (lower is better), with no free parameters fitted to those data. One attention and four interference-control experiments modelled.
limits: Rivals were simple. Cognitive-control tasks, not choice among reasoning methods. The model predicts blocking: a second cue carrying the same information did not add learning, as Bugg et al. found.
agent_relevance: Supports learning a value estimate from stimulus features over win-stay-lose-shift. Blocking warns that redundant routing cues add nothing.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, with commentaries (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 43)
finding: Search summaries (not the article) say commentators argued the method is mixed up with a claim that people truly are resource-rational (Rahnev), and that its normative status is unconvincing (Colombo). A teleology objection also appeared.
numbers: No numbers. The PDF download failed.
limits: Second-hand summary only. Unknown whether the authors' reply rebutted these points.
agent_relevance: Treat 'people are resource-rational' as a modelling stance and not a measured fact. Use it to design the agent, not to claim humans do this.

source: Callaway, Jain, van Opheusden, Das, Iwama, Gul, Krueger, Becker, Griffiths & Lieder (2022) Leveraging AI to improve people's planning strategies (PNAS 119(12))
finding: Exp 1: feedback on the quality of each planning step (metacognitive feedback) lifted test performance close to optimal. Feedback on actions did not help over plain practice.
numbers: N=151 (MTurk). Relative test score (0 chance, 100 optimal): no feedback 77.0, action feedback 73.5, metacognitive feedback 94.4. Meta vs none d=0.59, p=0.005. Action vs none d=-0.09, p=0.653. Kruskal-Wallis H=9.71, p=0.008.
limits: The no-feedback group was already at 77, so there is a ceiling. Scores were bimodal. Simple 3-step planning task. The tutor teaches how to plan, not which strategy to pick.
agent_relevance: What changed behaviour was a score on each reasoning step and not on the final answer. Suggests grading steps when learning a router.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) PNAS
finding: Training transferred to a harder five-step task and lasted 24 hours.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=297 Prolific): meta-feedback 81.2 points vs action feedback 49.0 (d=0.88, p<0.001) vs no feedback 57.6 (d=0.69, p<0.001). Delay retention H=28.66, p<0.001. Another transfer: 77.2 vs 63.0 (d=0.42, p=0.030) vs 59.0 (d=0.61, p=0.002).
limits: Transfer tasks kept the key structure (reward variance grows with distance). Online samples with exclusions (25 and 18 removed in two experiments).
agent_relevance: Strategy training can persist, but only where the new problem shares structure. Our features must capture that structure.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) PNAS
finding: Boundary condition: far transfer to a naturalistic road-trip task was weak. The authors say the estimate is likely an upper bound for real-world transfer.
numbers: Exp 5 (1380 recruited, 112 excluded): hotel-first rate on transfer 46.3% with meta-feedback vs 39.4% action feedback (d=0.17, P=0.035) vs 39.4% none (d=0.17, P=0.035) vs 23.5% video (d=0.61, P<0.001). Backward planning mediated the effect: indirect 12.9 points, 95% CI [7.6, 18.1], direct -3.8 [-8.0, 0.4].
limits: Small effect, p near .035. Backward-planning rate dropped sharply on the first transfer trial in all groups.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a learned strategy to carry to different-looking problems. Retrain or tag per task class.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) PNAS
finding: Both feedback parts are needed: a delay penalty for a poor step and a hint of what the best strategy would do. Neither works alone.
limits: Effect is smaller than Exp 1 (d=0.32 vs 0.59).
agent_relevance: A cost penalty plus a worked demonstration beat either alone. For an LLM: a token-cost term in the router reward and a worked example together.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) PNAS
finding: A passive video demonstration did worse than practice on far transfer.
numbers: Video group hotel-first 23.5% vs 39.4% to 46.3% for practice groups; video vs meta-feedback d=0.61, P<0.001.
limits: One transfer task. Why watching hurt is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Showing a strategy alone is poor. In-context examples likely need the model to act and then be scored.

source: Lieder, Callaway, Jain, Krueger, Das, Gul & Griffiths (2019) A cognitive tutor for helping people overcome present bias (RLDM)
finding: Early report of the same tutor: practice with feedback beat plain practice, held after 24 hours, and beat being told the principle. 38% of controls showed present bias on trial 1.
numbers: Exp 1 post-test 36.2 vs 24.6 dollars per trial, t(2258)=10.7, p<0.0001. Control near-optimal goal setting rose 0.0% to 26.4% over 30 trials (chi2(1)=16.1). Exp 4: tutor 38.0 vs told-only 24.2, t(83)=10.5. About 50 per condition.
limits: Workshop paper. The t test with df 2258 treats trials as independent, so the evidence is overstated. Later PNAS work used participant-level tests with smaller effects.
agent_relevance: Telling the strategy in words is weak. A system prompt describing a strategy is likely weaker than examples with step-level feedback.

source: Hierarchical planning strategy discovery and tutoring (arXiv 2102.00521)
finding: Demonstration tutors help only if the taught strategy fits the real task size. Earlier tutors limited to small tasks did not beat plain practice.
numbers: Exp 1, 42 per group, 7 excluded: hierarchical tutor 204.48 points/trial vs control 177.36 (p=.006, d=.304), vs feedback tutor 167.02 (p<.001, d=.40), vs non-hierarchical tutor (p=.025, d=.258). Feedback tutor vs control d=.104, p=.45. Non-hierarchical vs control d=.045, p=.67.
limits: Small samples, non-parametric tests. Strategies come from a task model, so a wrong model gives bad advice.
agent_relevance: A router built from a simplified task model can fail to help. Check the model matches real tasks.

source: Heindrich et al. (2023, v3 2025) An intelligent tutor for planning in large partially observable environments (arXiv 2302.02785)
finding: Pre-registered tutor test in a 60-node partially observable task. Tutored people matched the model strategy in score. A dummy tutor that showed the same environment did not help.
numbers: 330 recruited, 37 excluded. Median resource-rationality score: no tutor 11.46, choice tutor 22.67, model strategy 22.41 to 22.70 (tutor vs model p=.453). Group effect F(1.9,259.58)=33.22, p<.001; tutor vs none F(1)=57.90; tutor vs dummy F(1)=50.52; dummy vs none p<.29. Goal-first clicks: 84% (tutor).
limits: Abstract flight-planning game. The authors say it is not yet a real educational application.
agent_relevance: A random-strategy control is needed to show a learned policy beats mere exposure. Add a dummy-router control.

source: He & Lieder (2024) Experience-driven discovery of planning strategies (arXiv 2412.03111)
finding: Without a tutor, people rarely discover a new useful planning strategy. After 120 trials about 29% had it.
numbers: 420 recruited, 378 completed, 349 analysed. Adaptive-strategy share rose from 0.79% (CI [0, 2.22%]) on trial 1 to 28.57% (CI [27.21, 29.93]) on trial 120. Model comparison: 90% of people best fit by a learning model; REINFORCE-type 61%, mental-habit 39%, SSL-style under 1%.
limits: Task built so the strategy was unlikely known. Some participants labelled habitual did well because they inspected every node early.
agent_relevance: Discovery by trial and error is slow even for people. An agent should not count on finding better strategies from outcome feedback alone.

source: Jain et al. (2023) What are the mechanisms underlying metacognitive learning? (arXiv 2302.04840)
finding: 86 models of how people learn planning strategies were compared on 382 participants. Gradient-style learning (REINFORCE) won. Prior findings on the mechanism were inconsistent.
numbers: 86 models, 382 participants, two experiments. Non-learning model best for 34% of all participants and 25% after dropping non-learners. REINFORCE family best for 47.41% of learners.
limits: Mechanism still unsettled. Models miss an extra effort cost: people planned less than the resource-rational strategy.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one learning rule for the router. A gradient-style policy update is as good a bet as value tables.

source: He & Lieder (2025) Individual differences in the cognitive mechanisms of planning strategy discovery (arXiv 2505.23519)
finding: People differ in which learning mechanisms they use. Variants with extra mechanisms fit most people better than plain REINFORCE.
numbers: Variants fit 244 participants (69.96%) better than plain REINFORCE (102; 30.09%).
limits: Same dataset as the 2024 study, so not independent. Model fit does not prove mechanism.
agent_relevance: Individual differences are the norm. A portfolio of routing rules with a meta-selector fits this.

source: Hu, Roshan & Varma (2026) Are More Tokens Rational? Inference-Time Scaling in LMs as Adaptive Resource Rationality (arXiv 2602.10329)
finding: LLMs shift strategy as problem size grows: they enumerate pairs at small size and move to elimination as the space grows, with no explicit training for this. XOR tasks show less shift.
numbers: Variable-attribution task, 4 models (DeepSeek R1 and V3, Qwen3-Next-80B Thinking and Instruct). Strategy labels from a Kimi-K2 judge checked on 100 human-labelled cases. Reasoning models stay near-perfect as size grows; instruction models fall on XOR/XNOR; direct answer falls to chance. Qwen almost never uses elimination on XOR.
limits: One synthetic task. LLM judge for labels. Tokens counted as characters. Shows strategy tracks size, not rational cost-benefit.
agent_relevance: LLM strategy choice already follows problem size, but weakly on hard logic types. The scaffold should make the choice explicit there.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut & Griffiths (2024, v3 2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (arXiv 2410.05563)
finding: A value-of-computation reward (accuracy minus token cost) in expert iteration cuts tokens at equal or better accuracy. The trained model reasons longer on hard problems.
numbers: Output tokens: 35-42% fewer than few-shot prompting, 23-32% fewer than STaR. Out-of-domain MMLU-CF: 28-36% fewer than STaR at similar accuracy. Hard-vs-easy length gap up to 50.3% on Llama-3.2-3B. Tasks: ARC, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, ProofWriter.
limits: Needs fine-tuning. Small open models. The instruction-tuned CoT model did not adapt length to difficulty. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the Lieder-Griffiths idea in LLMs. Without training we can imitate it with a length budget per problem class.

source: Ong et al. (2024) RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data (arXiv 2406.18665)
finding: Routers trained on preference data send easy queries to a cheap model and cut cost by more than 2x. Weak routers work only on in-distribution queries.
numbers: MT Bench score 8.8 at CPT(50%) is 95% of GPT-4 (9.3). MMLU: routers trained on Arena data alone equal the random router; adding golden labels gives APGR gains up to about +20%.
quote: reducing costs by up to 75% as compared to the random router
limits: Strong/weak model pairs, not reasoning strategies. Out-of-distribution failure before augmentation. Judge-labelled data.
agent_relevance: Learned routers fail out of distribution. Fall back to the expensive path when features look unfamiliar.

source: Chen, Zaharia & Zou (2023) FrugalGPT (arXiv 2305.05176)
finding: A learned cascade of LLMs matches the best single model at much lower cost, or beats it at equal cost.
numbers: Up to 98% cost reduction at GPT-4-level performance, or +4% accuracy over GPT-4 at the same cost. API prices differ by two orders of magnitude.
limits: Per-dataset training. The cascade needs an answer scorer. Prices change.
agent_relevance: A cascade (try cheap, escalate on low score) is a cheap S0 that needs no feature engineering.

source: Fang, Ma & Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think (arXiv 2505.13379)
finding: An LLM can learn per query whether to use short or long reasoning. Vanilla GRPO collapsed to one mode; splitting the control-token and response losses fixed it.
numbers: Long-chain use cut by 50% to 90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500 and GSM8K (abstract). Table long-think shares range from 100.00% down to 2.35% across datasets and sizes.
limits: Training-based. Mode collapse is a documented failure of learned strategy selection.
agent_relevance: The collapse matches SSL lock-in in people. Force exploration of both modes.

source: Scheibehenne, Rieskamp & Wagenmakers (2013) Testing adaptive toolbox models: a Bayesian hierarchical approach (Psychological Review 120)
finding: Search summary of the abstract: Bayesian mixture-model tests let toolbox theories be compared with rivals and limit strategy sprawl. No results were read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Abstract only via search; full text not downloaded.
agent_relevance: A rival to single-process accounts; read before claiming people do or do not use many strategies.

source: Rieskamp & Otto (2006) SSL: Strategy selection learning in decision making (JEP: General)
finding: Per a search summary of the abstract, SSL says people learn strategy expectations by reinforcement and pick in proportion to them. Learning was supported in 4 studies.
numbers: No numbers read first-hand; the 2008 reanalysis and the 2015 paper quote Exp 1 details.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The baseline rival: a plain class-wide reward average. Our feature-based S0 must beat this to be worth the extra complexity.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) vs Rieskamp (2008): three rival theories compared
finding: Three theory families disagree: cost-benefit contingency (Beach & Mitchell 1978; Payne), reinforcement learning of average payoff (SSL, RELACS, SCADS), and feature-based rational metareasoning. Each fails at least one test.
numbers: Start-up: people begin with the costly strategy, against pure cost-benefit. Mixed environment: 64.6% vs 50%, against SSL and RELACS. No-feedback switching under time pressure: against SSL and RELACS. Slow switching after a change (27% and 65% switched): supports SSL-style lock-in.
limits: No single study runs all rivals on the same people. Metareasoning's start-up behaviour was fit to data and not predicted.
agent_relevance: A good router combines learning from reward, feature prediction and cost.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) vs Lieder et al. (2019): effect size drift
finding: Effects shrink as designs tighten and transfer grows. Workshop trial-level t=10.7; PNAS participant-level d=0.59 near, 0.88 and 0.69 delayed transfer, 0.42 and 0.61 other transfer, 0.32 component test, 0.17 far transfer.
numbers: d values: 0.59, 0.88, 0.69, 0.42, 0.61, 0.32, 0.17 (all from the PNAS paper).
limits: Different tasks and samples; not a formal meta-analysis. No independent-lab replication was found in the sources read.
agent_relevance: Expect any learned strategy to give roughly a third to a half of its first lab effect on a new task.
